headings.title: Introduction to Food Constituents and Nutritional Significance
headings.content: Food constituents refer to the various chemical substances found in foods that are essential for sustaining human life, promoting growth, and maintaining overall health. For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding these constituents is critical, as malnutrition remains a significant public health challenge across many communities. Food is broadly categorized into macro-nutrients and micro-nutrients, alongside water, dietary fiber, and non-nutritive bioactive compounds. Each constituent plays a unique physiological role, ranging from energy generation to structural building and metabolic regulation. When evaluating patients in clinical or community settings, nurses must recognize how dietary intake directly influences health outcomes, recovery from illness, and resistance to infections. Deficiencies or excesses in any of these components can precipitate disease states such as kwashiorkor, marasmus, scurvy, or chronic non-communicable diseases like diabetes and hypertension. Therefore, comprehensive patient assessment must include a thorough dietary history. By understanding the foundational principles of nutritional science, healthcare professionals can design effective dietary interventions, provide evidence-based health education, and advocate for nutritional security, especially among vulnerable populations such as pregnant women, infants, and the elderly.

headings.title: Macronutrients: Carbohydrates, Proteins, and Fats
headings.content: Macronutrients are the foundational nutrients required by the human body in large quantities to supply energy, support cellular repair, and maintain structural integrity. They are divided into three primary classes: carbohydrates, proteins, and fats. Carbohydrates serve as the body's primary and most rapid source of energy, yielding approximately four kilocalories per gram. They are classified into simple sugars and complex carbohydrates, the latter of which include starches vital for sustained stamina. Proteins are composed of amino acids, which are often termed the building blocks of life. They are essential for tissue growth, enzyme synthesis, hormone production, and immune function. Certain amino acids are termed essential because the human body cannot synthesize them, meaning they must be obtained directly from dietary sources like beans, meat, and fish. Fats, or lipids, provide the highest concentration of energy, yielding about nine kilocalories per gram, and are crucial for cellular membrane structure, fat-soluble vitamin absorption, and thermal insulation. In nursing practice, patient nutritional care plans must balance these three macronutrients to prevent energy deficits, muscle wasting, and metabolic disorders, ensuring optimal recovery and vitality.

headings.title: Micronutrients: Vitamins and Minerals
headings.content: Micronutrients comprise vitamins and minerals, which are required by the body in much smaller amounts than macronutrients but are nonetheless indispensable for health. Vitamins are organic compounds categorized into water-soluble (such as B-complex vitamins and vitamin C) and fat-soluble (such as vitamins A, D, E, and K). They act primarily as coenzymes, facilitating metabolic pathways, supporting vision, boosting immune response, and ensuring proper blood clotting. Minerals are inorganic elements further divided into macrominerals (like calcium, phosphorus, and potassium) and trace minerals (like iron, zinc, and iodine). They contribute to structural components, such as bone and teeth formation, and maintain fluid and electrolyte balance, nerve impulse transmission, and oxygen transport via hemoglobin. In Nigeria, micronutrient deficiencies—often referred to as hidden hunger—are prevalent, contributing to conditions like iron-deficiency anemia, goiter, and xerophthalmia. Nurses play a vital role in identifying signs of these deficiencies, educating patients on the inclusion of diverse local foods, and administering appropriate supplementation programs to safeguard public health.

headings.title: The Vital Role of Water in Human Nutrition
headings.content: Water is the most abundant and vital constituent of the human body, accounting for roughly 60% of total body weight in healthy adults. Despite yielding no energy, it is indispensable for survival, acting as the primary solvent for biochemical reactions, a medium for nutrient and waste transport, a lubricant for joints, and a key regulator of body temperature via perspiration. Nursing assessments must closely monitor hydration status, especially in vulnerable patient groups such as infants, the elderly, and those experiencing febrile illnesses, severe vomiting, or diarrhea. Dehydration can rapidly lead to electrolyte imbalances, hypovolemic shock, and acute kidney injury if left uncorrected. Conversely, fluid overload can precipitate pulmonary edema in patients with compromised cardiac or renal function. Nurses must calculate accurate fluid intake and output charts, promote oral rehydration therapy (ORT) during gastrointestinal infections, and understand the physiologic mechanisms of fluid balance. Educating patients and caregivers on the importance of clean, safe drinking water is also a fundamental preventive health measure taught in community nursing practice.

headings.title: Dietary Fiber and Gastrointestinal Health
headings.content: Dietary fiber consists of plant-based carbohydrate portions that are resistant to digestion and absorption in the human small intestine, passing relatively intact into the large bowel. Fiber is categorized into soluble fiber, which dissolves in water to form a gel-like substance that helps regulate blood glucose and cholesterol levels, and insoluble fiber, which adds bulk to stool and accelerates intestinal transit time. For nursing students, understanding fiber's role in gastrointestinal health is essential for managing conditions such as constipation, diverticular disease, and hemorrhoids. A high-fiber diet stimulates peristalsis, prevents fecal stasis, and nourishes beneficial gut microbiota through fermentation processes. Furthermore, fiber promotes satiety, which assists in body weight management and the prevention of obesity and type 2 diabetes. Nurses should encourage patients to incorporate fiber-rich local foods, such as whole grains, legumes, vegetables, and tubers, into their daily meals while ensuring adequate fluid intake to prevent fiber-induced intestinal blockage.

headings.title: Phytochemicals and Antioxidants in Plant-Based Foods
headings.content: Phytochemicals and antioxidants are non-nutritive bioactive chemical compounds naturally occurring in plant-based foods such as fruits, vegetables, nuts, and seeds. While not traditionally classified as essential nutrients, they play a profound protective role in human health by combating oxidative stress and neutralizing free radicals—unstable molecules that damage cell membranes, proteins, and DNA. Examples of well-known phytochemicals include carotenoids, flavonoids, and polyphenols, many of which give vibrant colors to local Nigerian fruits and vegetables like pawpaw, tomatoes, and dark leafy greens. Antioxidants help mitigate chronic systemic inflammation, lower the risk of cardiovascular disease, support immune defense, and offer protective effects against certain types of malignancies. In clinical practice, nurses should educate patients on the value of consuming a diverse, colorful diet rather than relying solely on isolated supplements. Understanding the synergy of whole plant foods empowers nurses to promote holistic wellness and preventative health strategies within their communities.

headings.title: Clinical Implications of Nutrient Deficiencies and Imbalances
headings.content: Clinical manifestations of nutrient deficiencies and imbalances present across a wide spectrum, reflecting the specific physiological roles of each missing or excessive constituent. Protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) manifests in pediatric populations as kwashiorkor (characterized by edema, apathy, and fatty liver due to severe protein shortage despite adequate calories) or marasmus (severe wasting from chronic caloric and protein deprivation). Micronutrient shortages produce distinct clinical syndromes, such as night blindness from vitamin A deficiency, beriberi from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, scurvy from vitamin C deficiency, and rickets from vitamin D or calcium imbalance. Conversely, nutritional excesses pose equally severe clinical challenges, leading to obesity, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, and hypertension. Nurses must maintain high clinical suspicion during patient assessments, identifying early warning signs such as integumentary changes, fatigue, poor wound healing, and growth retardation. By recognizing these clinical implications, nurses can initiate prompt dietary modifications, collaborate with clinical dietitians, and deliver targeted health education that alters disease trajectories.
